text: PhD applicants mostly apply on their own. The hard parts are finding advisors who actually fit, and ten programs with slightly different rules. HiOffer is an agent that does that work and shows its sources.

Six modules, one conversation: find programs, check requirements, assess advisors, assemble materials, support the process, track signals and decide offers. Each is a page you can manage, and things the agent does for you in chat.
Inside, HiOffer opens with a brief: three programs, eight verified advisors, nine to-dos due this month, and what to do next. The agent is ongoing, not just reactive.

Ask for the best-fit advisors at UW. The agent calls its tools, then answers with a card. Yulia Tsvetkov: identity anchored by two sources, recent papers verified on OpenAlex, and whether she says she is taking students.

Ask for the drafts. A statement within the limit, a fit paragraph per advisor, an outreach email each. Every sentence is tagged back to the applicant's files or a verified paper, and a verifier has checked them. You copy. HiOffer never sends.

The timeline holds what only a human can do: email each advisor, remind recommenders, pay and submit, dated from the official deadlines. Offers are compared with visible weights. Decision support, not a decision.

Every run is one neatlogs trace: a span per sub-agent and per tool call, with tokens and latency. Run one died on a malformed JSON reply; the trace shows the exact error. In run three the verifier caught the writer inventing a paper, and the trace led to the real bug: my OpenAlex filter had dropped the professor's real papers.
A neatlogs detection then caught a connector span failing silently inside run five. Fixed the same hour. Pruning old tool results halved input tokens per call.

Entire recorded every coding session behind every commit: twenty-eight checkpoints in a day. Checkpoint explain shows the intent and the files; entire why traces one line of code back to the conversation that wrote it.

Pricing comes from the traces: about two dollars of model time per program. In cfo.ai, a forty-nine dollar season pass needs cost under nineteen sixty for a sixty percent margin. One surprise: with sales peaking in autumn, a hundred-fifty-thousand-dollar raise runs out of cash before year two's peak, while bootstrapping needs a nine-hundred-dollar bridge.
Everything is public: the repo, the build log with every failure, the traces, the plan. HiOffer, built in public for neatHack.
